what_its_for: Diclofenac epolamine is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) that comes as a patch you wear on your skin. It is used to relieve pain, swelling, and tenderness caused by minor injuries such as sprains, strains, and bruises (also called acute minor soft tissue injuries).
how_to_take: This medication is a patch that you apply directly to the skin over the painful area. Before applying, clean and dry your skin. Peel off the backing and press the sticky side firmly onto the skin. Wash your hands with soap and water after touching the patch. Wear the patch for 12 hours, then remove it and apply a fresh one. Do not cut the patch into smaller pieces. Do not apply the patch to broken, damaged, irritated, or infected skin. Do not cover the patch with bandages, plastic wrap, or tight clothing. Do not apply more than one patch at a time unless your doctor tells you otherwise.
dosing: The usual dose is one patch applied to the most painful area twice a day — once in the morning and once in the evening (every 12 hours). Always follow the dosing instructions your doctor or pharmacist gives you. Do not use more patches than prescribed or wear them for longer than directed.
missed_dose: If you forget to apply a patch at the scheduled time, apply one as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next patch, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not apply two patches at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store the patches at room temperature, away from heat and direct sunlight. Keep them in the original sealed envelope until you are ready to use them. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. After removing a used patch, fold it in half with the sticky sides together and dispose of it safely in the trash, away from children and animals, as used patches still contain active medication.
what_to_avoid: Do not get the patch wet — avoid swimming, bathing, showering, or using a hot tub while wearing it. Do not expose the patch to heat sources such as heating pads, electric blankets, or heat lamps, as this can increase the amount of medication absorbed into your body. Avoid using other NSAIDs (such as ibuprofen or naproxen) at the same time unless your doctor approves. Avoid applying sunscreen, lotions, or cosmetics to the same area as the patch. Limit alcohol consumption, as it may increase the risk of stomach bleeding.
when_to_call_doctor: Contact your doctor right away or seek emergency medical care if you experience any of the following: chest pain, shortness of breath, or weakness on one side of your body (signs of a heart attack or stroke); black, tarry, or bloody stools, or vomiting blood (signs of stomach bleeding); severe skin reactions such as blisters, rash, or peeling skin at or around the patch site; swelling of your face, lips, tongue, or throat; difficulty breathing or swallowing; unusual weight gain or swelling in your hands, feet, or ankles; or signs of kidney or liver problems such as decreased urination, yellowing of the skin or eyes, or severe stomach pain.
when_it_works: You may start to feel some pain relief within a few hours of applying the first patch. However, it may take a day or two before you notice the full benefit. This medication is meant for short-term use. If your pain does not improve after a few days, talk to your doctor.
special_populations: Older adults (age 65 and over) may be at higher risk for side effects such as stomach bleeding, kidney problems, and heart-related issues — use with caution and only as directed by a doctor. Pregnant women should avoid this medication, especially during the last 3 months of pregnancy, as it may harm the unborn baby. Talk to your doctor before using if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. This patch has not been studied for safety and effectiveness in children and is generally not recommended for use in patients under 18 years of age.
